text: In InnoDB every secondary-index entry stores the row's primary-key columns, so the primary key's size is paid again in every secondary index. MySQL's docs: 'If the primary key is long, the secondary indexes use more space, so it is advantageous to have a short primary key.'
why: Shows exactly why a 16-byte UUID primary key bloats every index, not just one.

text: InnoDB caches index and table pages in its buffer pool as they are read and evicts least-recently-used pages when it needs room. By default MySQL saves the most recently used 25% of buffer-pool pages at shutdown and reloads them at startup to shorten warm-up.
why: Corrects the idea that all indexes are loaded and pinned in RAM at boot.

text: A query avoids reading table rows only when the index covers every column it needs (an index-only or covering scan). Otherwise PostgreSQL fetches each matching row from the table during the scan, often with random I/O.
why: Explains when 'everything happens on the index' is true, and how to make it true (covering indexes).

text: REPLACE takes every column from the statement and sets any column you don't list to its default. Because it deletes the old row, it also fires DELETE triggers as well as INSERT triggers.
why: The practical reason REPLACE and ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE are not interchangeable.

text: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE reports 1 affected row for an insert, 2 for an update, and 0 if the row was already identical. MySQL advises avoiding it on tables with more than one unique index, because only one matching row is updated.
why: Lets readers tell inserts from updates and avoid a known pitfall.

text: Flickr's published ticket server actually uses REPLACE INTO Tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a'); SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();. Because REPLACE deletes and re-inserts the single stub row, each call produces a fresh AUTO_INCREMENT id.
why: The source for this case study uses REPLACE, and its delete-plus-insert is what yields new IDs.

text: MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT works on any integer type: INT is 4 bytes (unsigned max about 4.29 billion) and BIGINT is 8 bytes. When the type's maximum is reached, the next insert fails. Flickr's ticket table uses bigint unsigned.
why: Gives the real ID sizes and the overflow behaviour.

text: PostgreSQL never hands back a nextval value: it is not reused even if the transaction aborts, so sequences can have gaps and the docs say they 'cannot be used to obtain "gapless" sequences'.
why: Readers should expect gaps in sequence-generated IDs.

text: MySQL 8.4 writes the auto-increment counter to the redo log on every change and to the data dictionary at checkpoints, so it survives restarts, though reuse after an unexpected exit is not guaranteed. PostgreSQL sequences can pre-allocate values in memory per session (CACHE); unused cached values are lost when the session ends, leaving holes.
why: Concrete examples of 'the database optimises persistence' and its gap trade-off.

text: In PostgreSQL, a serial column is shorthand for CREATE SEQUENCE tablename_colname_seq plus a column default of nextval('tablename_colname_seq'), with the sequence owned by the column.
why: Shows the hidden sequence the teacher describes.

text: Instagram ran PostgreSQL, and each logical shard was a Postgres schema (e.g. insta5) holding the same set of tables. Several thousand of these were mapped in code to far fewer physical servers.
why: Grounds the logical-shard idea in what Instagram actually built.

text: PostgreSQL's docs warn that rows skipped by OFFSET 'still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient', which is why deep LIMIT/OFFSET pagination gets slow.
why: Primary-source backing for the limit-offset point.
